To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

calcifying sites in the sclerites and the axial skeleton of the red octocorals Corallium rubum were surrounded by calcifying medium that was not pH up-regulation with respect to the seawater, contrary what is observed in the scleractinains.
the calcifying media in red octocoral are not pH upregulated, but rather are alkaline relative to the calcifying cells and the gastrovascular canals.
pH at calcification site is alkaline but not pH up-regulation, and that this is consistent with sensitivity to acidification.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the biomineralization of a calcareous octocoral and the results are relevant to our understanding of biomineralization in calcareous octacorals in general and in corals in particular, and to the potential effects of ocean acidification on this important calcifier.
the first in vivo pH measurement in an octocorallian species and provides insights into the biomineralization of calcareous octocorallians.
a fundamental aspect of biomineralization, the control of pH at calcification site, which is of relevance to the physiology of calcification and the impact of ocean acidification.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the pH at the sites of calcification in C. rubrum is not up-regulated, and therefore the species is potentially sensitive to ocean acidifcation.
pH in the calcification site of red corals is not up-regulated compared to seawater.
pH at the site of sclerite formation in C. rubrum is not upregulated compared to seawater pH, which is in contrast with pH regulation in scleractinia.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the calcifying media are not alkaline, but are more alkaline than the calcifying cells and gastrovascular fluids.
pH at sites of calcification in red coral is not up-regulated with reference to seawater.
pH in the calcifying medium of C. rubrum is not up-regulated with reference to surrounding fluids and seawater.
The main takeaway from our work is that
pH measurements at the calcification site are essential to assess the biomineralization capacity of calcifiers in the ocean.
in vivo pH imaging of calcification sites can be used to understand the calcification physiology of calcifiers, and that the pH up-regulation mechanism of scleractinias is not universal in corals.
in situ pH measurements at calcification sites are a prerequisite to understanding the biomineralization mechanisms of calcifiers.
